newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral embarrassed by insurance setback.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral embarrassed by insurance setback.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral suffered a humiliating setback on Wednesday when his minority government failed to muster enough votes in parliament to defeat an amendment barring foreign insurance firms.
Gujral abruptly withdrew an insurance regulatory bill when it became clear his government did not have enough votes to defeat the opposition-backed amendment.

"We withdraw the bill," Gujral told the lower house, the Lok Sabha, after the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) pressed for a vote on the amendment barring foreign multinational companies from the insurance sector.
Coalition partners said Gujral's government had been dealt an embarrassing blow by failing to rally enough support to push through the bill.

It aimed to create an Insurance Regulatory Authority to oversee the state-controlled insurance industry, and was considered an important first step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to private competition, both Indian and foreign.
Foreign insurance firms were shocked at the outcome and said it would send wrong signals about India's liberalisation credentials.

"The whole issue goes much wider than just insurance, which is only one part of it, and we wonder whether this sends a signal on overall liberalisation," said George Otto, chief representative at the India liaison office of Allianz AG Holdings.

A senior Finance Ministry official said the decision to withdraw the bill sent a worrisome signal to foreign investors who were counting on the gradual opening up of India's financial services sector.
Opposition members said the government was buckling under pressure from the United States and other Western nations to open up India's huge and potentially lucrative insurance sector.
"We know that the Americans are exerting pressure on you," said Samata party leader George Fernandez, a BJP ally.
"I don't want this house to be a surrogate of a foreign power," said Fernandez.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said there was no proposal to allow a foreign company or a multinational into the insurance sector. But his assurances failed to pacify angry opposition members.
Chidambaram later told reporters after Gujral retracted the bill that the government would put forward a new one. "We will come back after resolving this narrow area of difference."
Communist parties, key allies in Gujral's fractious 15-party coalition, said Gujral had suffered a humiliating setback.
"It is an embarrassment, and Chidambaram is responsible for it," said Communist Party of India leader Gurudas Dasgupta.

Earlier on Wednesday, the lower house had rejected an amendment proposed by the Communist Party of India-Marxist, which is part of Gujral's coalition, to bar private firms from the insurance sector. The amendment was defeated by a 228-to-43 vote in the 545-seat house.
The government proposed in its 1997/98 (April-March) budget to open the health insurance sector to a small number of private Indian companies.

"The attempt to invite foreign companies just like the East India Company has been foiled," jubilant BJP lawmaker Ghumanmal Lodha told Reuters, referring to the business interests that led to two centuries of British colonial rule in the subcontinent.
